p2.t: For a hundred years the walls have held. People stop noticing a thing like that. They simply live inside it.

a1.t: There you are. I was about to come in with a bucket of water.

choices.t: “I had that dream again. The one about the outside.”
“Sorry. I’ll be ready in a minute.”

a_dream.t: The outside. Of course it is. You know most people on this street would call that a nightmare.

a_bread.t: Spoken like someone with sense. Which is exactly why you’re going to fetch some.

a_duty.t: No need to apologise. Just move.

a4.t: Marta in the Old Square is holding a loaf for us. We owe her for last week, so be polite and don’t count the change.

a4b.t: I’ll meet you at the gate square before noon. The Garrison is gathering a crowd for something.

a6q.t: Nothing’s happened. That’s the whole point of the Garrison, isn’t it? Nothing ever happens.

a6go.t: Me? Late? Go, before the bread’s gone.

a7.t: Stay on the main streets. This district is bigger than it feels.

a8s.t: And {player}, whatever the Garrison says today, stay where I can find you.

fx.text: Follow the marker to the Old Square.

a8p.t: And {player}, don’t wander. I mean it.

fx.text: Follow the marker to the Old Square.

a8f.t: And try not to get lost staring at the sky again.

fx.text: Follow the marker to the Old Square.

i1.t: Go on. I’ll be here. I’m always here.

o1.t: Mind the bucket. This well has been in a mood since spring.

choices.t: “Do you ever think about what’s past the wall?”

o3.t: Past the wall? I think about my knees. What’s out there is the Titans’ business, and they can keep it.

o4.t: A hundred years, and not one has climbed that gate. That’s the only fact an old man needs.

i1.t: Still here. So is the well.
Not now, dear, my hands are full of dough. Come back when someone’s sent you.
Go on, they’ll be waiting for that loaf.

m1.t: There’s my best customer’s best runner. Let me guess. Bread, on credit?

m2a.t: {anchor} must have been kind to you this morning. You look like someone who was asked nicely.

m2b.t: {anchor} sent you off in a hurry, I suppose. Never mind. Hand me the basket.

m3.t: One loaf, still warm. And tell them the debt is forgiven until harvest. I am not made of stone.

m5a.t: Go on, then. And if you see those three children by the plaza, tell them to stay out of the canal.

m5b.t: Greedy! Half a loaf, then, for whoever’s standing in the sun at the gate. Don’t tell anyone.

k1.t: Three children sit on the edge of the plaza with a battered book open between them.

k2.t: …and the sea is salt water. Not a river, not a lake. A whole sea, bigger than all the land inside the walls.

k3.t: Say it again. Slower. Then tell me why nobody here wants to see it.

k4.t: Because they’re afraid. Eren, you’re being loud again.

k6a.t: Then you’re one of us. Don’t tell the adults.

k6b.t: Safe isn’t the same as free.

k6c.t: Drawings. Ships. A place where the water burns orange at sunset. I’ve read it so many times the spine is giving up.

k8.t: The children go back to their argument, quieter now. For a moment the plaza feels very small.

i1.t: Shh. I’m at the good part.

h1.t: Hic. Oh. Don’t look at me like that, I’m on duty. Technically.

choices.t: “Is it true nothing ever comes over the wall?”
“Should you be drinking at the gate?”

h3.t: True? It’s the only thing that’s ever been true. A hundred years of nothing. You know what that does to a man? Makes him very, very thirsty.

h4.t: If one ever did show up, I’d like to think I’d be sober enough to do something about it. I’d like to think a lot of things.

h_no.t: Should I? No. Do I? Every day. Don’t tell the Commander.

i1.t: Move along, move along. Nothing to see. Nothing ever happens.

g1.t: {anchor} is waiting near the gate with a hand over {anchor.his} eyes, looking up at the wall.

g2.t: Bread? Good. Now look up. Really look.

g3.t: Fifty metres of grey stone. The Garrison says it will outlast everything. Nobody asks what it is meant to outlast.

g4.t: Do you ever feel it? That we’re not living here. We’re being kept.

g6a.t: Maybe it is. I’d like it to be.

g6b.t: Then I’m coming with you. Don’t argue.

g6c.t: You and your stomach. Fine. Sit.

g7.t: Somewhere above you, the light changes.

b1.t: The ground jumps. Dust falls from the gate’s arch like flour from a torn sack.

b2.t: Above the wall, where there was sky, there is a face.

choices.t: Seize {anchor}’s hand and run for the boats.
Run, and shout for {anchor} to follow.
Stand still. Your legs will not move.

b5.t: This is as far as the current build goes. The escape through Shiganshina is built next, and your choice has been saved.

d1.t: The lamp is lit by the time you reach home. {anchor} is stirring something that smells like onions and patience.

d2.t: You’re late, and you’re warm, which means you took the long way. Give me the bread.

d3x.t: Half a loaf extra? Marta’s been giving you things. What did you do, charm her?

d4.t: Sit. Eat. Tell me one thing you saw today that wasn’t on the way to anywhere.

choices.t: “The children by the plaza. They’re reading about the sea.”
“Hannes, asleep on his feet at the gate.”

d6a.t: The sea. Salt water, all the way to the edge of the world. I used to dream about that, too.

d6b.t: Asleep on duty? Then thank the stones they’ve never been tested.

d6c.t: A normal day. Hold on to that phrase. Most people don’t know it’s a gift until it’s gone.

d7.t: You eat. The lamp ticks. Outside, the district settles into its evening noises, and the wall stands over all of it, patient as a mountain.

d8.t: Bed. Tomorrow I need you at the gate before the heat. Go.

fx.text: Day 1 complete. Sleep to begin Day 2.

a1.t: Up. Good. There’s something I need you to carry for me.

a2.t: Hannes at the gate forgot his lunch again. Take him this pail. Don’t let him share it with the pigeons.

a4q.t: Because you’re the only one in this house who walks fast and listens slowly. It’s a useful combination.

a4t.t: He won’t. But he’ll remember who brought it. Soldiers are like cats that way.

a5.t: And if Oswin at the well wants to talk, let him. He says the wall hums at night. Nobody else will listen.

fx.text: Day 2. Take the lunch pail to Hannes at the gate.

h1.t: Is that, ah. Is that cabbage? Bless whoever sent it. Bless you, too, you walk-on-water little postman.

h2.t: Sit a minute. Watch the gate with me. It’s the best view in the district for nothing happening.

choices.t: “Why is there a second watch tonight?”
“What do you do if something happens?”

h4a.t: Doubled, is it? Orders. Somebody up the chain got a bad feeling. Don’t let it rattle you, kid. Chains get bad feelings every spring.

h4b.t: Every day. Boredom is the soldier’s whole job. The rest of it is waiting for the day boredom stops, and praying it doesn’t.

h4c.t: Happens? Then I do the thing I trained for. And I find out whether the training was worth it. I’d rather not find out.

h5.t: Go on. Stand by the gate a while if you want. Look at it properly. It’s older than any of us.

fx.text: Linger near the gate and watch.

h1.t: Hum? From the wall? Who’s been telling you that, old Oswin?

h2.t: …We hear it. Night watch hears it. Low, like a cart a long way off that never arrives. Command says it’s the stone settling.

h4a.t: Stone doesn’t usually settle on a rhythm. I’m going to go on telling myself it does.

h4b.t: Someone was told. That’s why the watch doubled. Don’t repeat it, all right?

h5.t: Tell Oswin he’s not mad. Don’t tell him I said so.

k1.t: You were at the gate? Did you see how many soldiers are on the wall?

k2.t: Doesn’t matter how many. A hundred soldiers sitting on a wall is still just a hundred people sitting.

choices.t: “Twice as many as usual, and they’re nervous.”
“Hannes says the wall hums at night.”

k4a.t: Nervous. Of what? I read that the Garrison hasn’t drawn a blade in anger in a century.

k4b.t: Bored. That’s what I wrote down too. Oh well.

k4c.t: A humming wall. …Eren, stop grinning, it isn’t a joke.

k5.t: I don’t care what it hums. One day I’m going to be on the other side, and then I’ll know.

k6.t: Come on. Your {anchor.rel} will be waiting. It’ll be dark soon.

e1.t: {anchor} is on the doorstep when you get home, one hand shading the last of the light.

e2.t: You’re quiet. That’s either hunger or thinking. Which is it?

e4a.t: Different how? No. Don’t answer. Come in, eat, and tell me with food in you. Things look smaller that way.

e4b.t: Good. A simple answer. I almost wish I had one of those.

e5.t: Tomorrow there’s the market. Marta’s promised me ribbons for the stall. And then the whole district will be out. Get some rest.

o1.t: You. Child. Come here. Listen, no, not with your ears. Put your hand on the stone.

o2.t: Feel that? No? Then wait for night. The wall hums. Low. Like a very large animal breathing.

o4a.t: Wind. Wind comes and goes. This one stays. Think it over.

o4b.t: Would you? Good. They’ll lie to you politely, but ask anyway.

o5.t: If anyone knows, it’s the man who stands by that gate every day. Ask Hannes.

o3a.t: He admitted it? Then I’m not mad. Thank you, child. I’ve waited a month for somebody to say that.

o3b.t: He said it was the stone? Of course he did. Well, stone’s patient.

o4.t: Keep your eyes open, whatever it is. There are worse things than being thought a fool by sensible people.

a1.t: Market day. The street outside is already loud with carts and bargaining, and for once the sky is the clean blue of a well-washed plate.

a2.t: Marta has ribbons set aside for the stall. Go and get them. Then I want you to find those three children, the dreamers.

a4a.t: Because it’s a good day to be near people who still want something from the world.

a4b.t: Of course you will. Don’t go empty-handed. People remember small kindnesses longer than large ones.

a5.t: Then meet me at the gate square when the sun is high. We’ll watch the crowd together.

fx.text: Day 3. Buy the ribbons from Marta.

m1.t: Ribbons! Blue, red, and a green one I’m not sure about. Take them all. Take two loaves for the children. They always look hungry.

m3a.t: Silly. I only bake bread. Go on, don’t let it cool.

m3b.t: Need? A bigger oven and a smaller creditor. Otherwise I’m a lucky woman.

m4.t: The whole district’s out today. It feels like a festival. Funny. It always feels like that just before something.

k1.t: The three of them are sitting on the plaza steps in the sun. The book is open between them again.

k2.t: You brought bread! Eren, move your boots, there’s a person here.

choices.t: Hold some back. You may need it.

k4a.t: Thank you. Everyone has the same. That’s fair.

k4b.t: …Thank you. You’ve noticed I haven’t eaten.

k4c.t: Cheapskate! Kidding. Everyone does that when they’re scared of running out.

k5.t: When I get to the sea I’m going to send a message back. A real one, in a bottle. Maybe you’ll find it.

k6.t: He’s not going alone. None of us is. Right?

k8a.t: Then it’s a promise. I don’t forget promises.

k8b.t: That’s the most depressing thing anyone’s ever said to me. Great. Thanks.

k9.t: The sun is warm on the stones. For a moment, there is nothing in the world but four people and a loaf of bread.
